Name: Suncoast Charging, Land O' Lakes
Milestone: First third-party-owned Tesla Superchargers in North America
Summary: Suncoast Charging installed the first third-party-owned Tesla Superchargers in North America. Built and serviced by Tesla, owned and operated by Suncoast.
Notes: Stall count is not stated in this article. A later EVwire post describes the site as four wrapped Superchargers, but that is a cross-reference, not this article, so stalls stays null here.

Name: Suncoast Charging, Wesley Chapel
Summary: Suncoast revealed stall wraps featuring four threatened Florida species at its Wesley Chapel site, each stamped with a Preserve and Protect seal.
Unstated: stalls, status, hardware, power_kw, address, opened_on
Notes: The article counts four designs, not four stalls. Status is genuinely unstated: the piece never says whether the site is built or operating. Do not upgrade either without a source.

Name: Diamonds by Raymond Lee
Summary: Custom-branded Tesla V4 Superchargers being installed at a luxury jeweller, alongside a dual-port ChargePoint unit. Deployed by EnviroSpark Energy Solutions.
Notes: Status was Construction as of April 2026. Not re-verified since.

Name: Francis Energy at Crest Foods, Norman
Milestone: First Francis Energy site with Tesla Superchargers, and the first time a direct competitor to the Tesla network deployed Tesla hardware on its own network
Summary: Francis Energy reopened its Norman site with four Tesla Superchargers, priced at $0.44/kWh for all drivers. Developed with GoodFinch.
Notes: Article published one day before the stated 13 Jan opening, but says the site was already live on Tesla's map and app.

Name: Francis Energy, N Lincoln Blvd
Address: N Lincoln Blvd, Oklahoma City, OK
Summary: Permit documents filed by Francis Energy and Amp Engineering show Tesla hardware for a site on N Lincoln Blvd.
Notes: Permit-stage only. Evidence grade C. May since have been folded into the 17-site Francis aggregate.

Name: Francis Energy, Bartlesville
Summary: Eight Supercharger units installed but not yet commissioned as of January 2026, per a Tesla Motors Club thread.
Notes: Forum-sourced. Likely commissioned by now and inside the 17-site aggregate, but not separately confirmed.

Name: Francis Energy, Durant
Summary: Francis-labelled Superchargers being installed as of mid-December 2025, apparently replacing the site's BTCPower chargers.
Notes: Likely commissioned by now and inside the 17-site aggregate, but not separately confirmed.

Name: Alpharetta Department of Public Safety
Milestone: First city in the world to buy Tesla Superchargers
Summary: Four 325 kW city-branded Superchargers next to the police department, open to the public and to the force's two Model Ys. One pull-in accessible stall.
Notes: This article says 325 kW but never says V4. Three later EVwire posts refer back to Alpharetta as V4. Hardware left null because the source article does not state it.

Name: ChargedEV Hubs at Global Mall
Milestone: First Supercharger for Business deployment in Georgia from a private company
Summary: Eight V4 stalls at 325 kW with Magic Dock along I-85, reported at a 2.5 MWh/day run rate. Delivered with Car Charger Specialists, Tesla Energy and Georgia Power.

Name: Courtyard FBG TX
Milestone: Fredericksburg's first and only Tesla Supercharger
Summary: Eight V4 stalls at up to 325 kW in a courtyard with a boutique grocer, champagne lounge, events venue, wine bar and dog park.

Name: Texas Best Smokehouse, Midlothian
Milestone: Appears to be Victron Energy's first Supercharger for Business site
Summary: Eight V4 stalls up to 325 kW, one accessible, at a Texas Best Smokehouse travel center just off US-287.
Notes: The first-site claim is hedged in the article as "appears to be". Victron Energy here is the travel-center operator behind Texas Best Smokehouse, not the Dutch power-electronics company of the same name.

Name: AC Customs Supercharger
Milestone: A rare V3 site on the programme
Summary: Four V3 stalls up to 250 kW, 24/7, at $0.43/kWh for Tesla and non-Tesla alike. AC Customs said these were some of Tesla's last V3 units, discounted to clear stock.

Name: Genoa Golf Club
Milestone: One of the first privately owned Tesla Supercharger sites in the western US
Summary: Eight V4 stalls developed with Tesla Energy and Trout Electric, with a public ribbon-cutting on 8 May 2026. A later article describes the site as eight V4 Superchargers plus six Level 2 chargers.
Notes: Naming is inconsistent across sources: the April article says Genoa Golf Club, its own SEO field says Genoa Ranch Golf Course, and the August United Chargers Network piece says Genoa Lakes Golf Course. Kept the April body's name. The UCN article does not explicitly state that UCN owns this site, so operator stays as the club.

Name: HiON, Denver Tech Center
Summary: Four V4 stalls up to 325 kW, NACS and CCS, open 24/7, in the Denver Tech Center. HiON calls its stalls the world's first supercharging franchise on the Tesla network.
Notes: Greenwood Village is absent from the city-centroid dataset. Coordinates here are the mean of ZIP 80111 and 80112 centroids (the two core Greenwood Village / Denver Tech Center ZIPs) from midwire/free_zipcode_data. Lower confidence than the other pins.

Name: Little General travel center, Columbia
Summary: Four V4 stalls up to 325 kW with Magic Docks at Little General's new travel center just off Interstate 70.

Name: Grand Island Blvd Supercharger
Address: 1738 Grand Island Blvd, Grand Island, NY
Summary: Four V4 stalls with NACS, CCS and an ADA-accessible stall, off the Grand Island Bridge between Buffalo and Niagara Falls. Ribbon-cutting held 7 August 2026.
Notes: The site was under construction when first published on 13 July and the post was updated on 7 August with the ribbon-cutting.

Name: Island Center, Isle of Palms
Address: 1507 Palm Boulevard, Isle of Palms, SC
Milestone: South Carolina's first Supercharger for Business site
Summary: Four V4 Magic Dock stalls up to 325 kW, designed and built by Dominion Energy South Carolina under its turnkey programme for a site host who paid the full cost.
Notes: Dominion's logo is on the cabinets because Dominion built the station, but Dominion says the site host paid the full cost. Dominion is the delivery partner, not the owner. The host entity is never named beyond the venue.

Name: EVIO Charging, New York
Milestone: First privately owned Tesla Supercharger site in New York, described by the installer as the first in the Northeast
Summary: Powerup EV Solutions completed an eight-stall Tesla Supercharger turnkey for EVIO Charging, with a ribbon-cutting scheduled for 20 May 2026.
Notes: The article never names a city, only the state and "the Northeast", so this record has no coordinates and is deliberately excluded from the map. It appears in the site list with a location-unknown flag. Stall count comes from an image caption.

Name: Gorham Citgo
Summary: Four-stall site whose owner says it will close on 25 October unless New Hampshire restores the discontinued EV-2 electricity rate. Demand charges reported above $9,000 a month.
Notes: SOURCE IS AN UNPUBLISHED DRAFT as of 13 Aug 2026. Do not publish this pin until the article goes live. The $9,000/month figure is the owner's characterisation; one specific bill shown totals $13,211.

Name: EV Auto dealership, Brentwood
Summary: Branded Tesla Superchargers shown close to finished in a video at EV Auto's Brentwood dealership, the first of a claimed 20-plus locations in development.
Notes: Seen in a video only. The article says it will update when the site opens.

Name: bp pulse electric truck depot, Ontario
Milestone: bp Pulse's first US public electric-truck charging site
Summary: Two 750 kW Tesla MCS pull-through bays alongside four 400 kW CCS bays at bp Pulse's first US public e-truck depot.
Unstated: opened_on, address, whether this falls under Supercharger for Business
Notes: HEAVY-DUTY CLASS, NOT SUPERCHARGER FOR BUSINESS. This is Tesla MCS / Megacharger hardware for Class 6-8 trucks under bp's separate 2023 Tesla deal. The article never places it under the Supercharger for Business programme. Kept on the map as a separate heavy-duty layer, off by default.
